match.reason: The brief teaches where the heavier elements come from, through fusion inside stars, and no bank point covers that; the big bang card is related but only covers the early universe and the formation of atoms.

note:
A fresh check found these problems in this version. Fix each one, and keep everything that is right:
- Card, fact: 'Heavier elements, such as iron, form only in much more massive stars' is not strictly true. Much of the universe's iron comes from Type Ia supernovae (exploding white dwarfs), not only from massive stars. Elements heavier than iron mostly form by neutron capture, some of it in lower-mass stars, rather than by fusion. Drop 'only', e.g. 'Heavier elements, such as iron, form in much more massive stars.'

rejected.title: Where elements come from
card: Soon after the Big Bang, the universe was very hot and then cooled. The first nuclei that formed in this time were mostly hydrogen and helium.
Gravity pulled clouds of hydrogen and helium together to form stars. Inside a star, the core is hot and dense enough for nuclei to join together. This joining is called fusion.
In stars, fusion turns hydrogen into helium. Later in a star's life, helium can fuse into carbon and oxygen. Heavier elements, such as iron, form only in much more massive stars.
When some stars end their lives, they spread these elements into space. New stars and planets can then form from this material, including the Earth.
rejected.remember: Hydrogen and helium came first. Fusion in stars made heavier elements.

a.q: Which elements formed soon after the Big Bang?
opts: Hydrogen and helium
Carbon and oxygen
Helium and iron
Hydrogen and carbon
a.why: Mainly hydrogen and helium formed in the early universe. Carbon, oxygen and iron formed later, when fusion in stars joined smaller nuclei into larger ones.
a.clue: Think of the two lightest elements.

b.q: Oxygen in the air in Orange, NSW, is a heavier element. Where did its atoms first form?
opts: By fusion inside stars long ago
In the first moments after the Big Bang
By gravity pulling gas into the Earth
By fission in the Earth's crust
b.why: Heavier elements such as oxygen formed by fusion inside stars, then were spread into space when stars ended their lives. They did not form soon after the Big Bang. Gravity gathered this material into the Earth, but it did not make the elements.
b.clue: Which process builds heavier nuclei from lighter ones?

problems.detail: Why (a) says 'Only hydrogen and helium formed in the early universe', but tiny amounts of lithium also formed then. The card avoids 'only'. Suggest 'Mainly hydrogen and helium'.

'Over time, in larger stars, it builds heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen' suggests only larger stars make carbon and oxygen. Sun-like stars also fuse helium into carbon and oxygen. It is elements heavier than these that need massive stars.
